html:
Elmina Castle is a fort that the Portuguese built in 1482 at Elmina, on the coast of present-day Ghana, then called the Gold Coast. They named it São Jorge da Mina, St George of the Mine. It was the first European trading post on the Gulf of Guinea and is the oldest European building still standing south of the Sahara.

The Portuguese wanted to buy gold directly from Akan traders inland, rather than through the merchants of the trans-Saharan trade. Much of the stone and timber was shipped out ready-cut from Portugal.

At first the fort traded cloth, brass and beads for gold. Over time it became a major station of the Atlantic slave trade. Captives were held in its dungeons, sometimes for weeks, before being loaded onto ships for the Americas.

The Dutch West India Company took the castle in 1637 and held it until 1872, when the Dutch handed their Gold Coast forts to Britain. It then served the British colony until Ghana's independence in 1957. Today it is a museum, listed with the other forts and castles of Ghana as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and many visitors from the African diaspora come to see it.
